passages.text: Pathogenic Foodborne Bacteria in the Game Meat of Hunted Large Ungulates-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
ABSTRACT

Zoonotic bacterial pathogens are a major concern for food safety, yet information regarding their occurrence in game meat remains fragmented. <sentence_start/>This systematic review synthesizes available data on <italic>Salmonella</italic> spp., Shiga toxin-producing <italic>Escherichia coli</italic> (STEC), <italic>Listeria</italic> spp., <italic>Yersinia</italic> spp., and <italic>Campylobacter</italic> spp. in game meat from hunted wild ungulates. <sentence_start/>Relevant studies published between 2004 and 2024 were identified through structured database searches and screened using predefined criteria. <sentence_start/>Data on host species, diagnostic methods, prevalence estimates, isolate characterization, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) were extracted. <sentence_start/>Pooled prevalence estimates were determined, stratified by detection methods (culture-based and PCR-based) and animal groups (suids and ruminants). <sentence_start/>A total of 46 publications (170 studies; 223 prevalence estimates) were included. <sentence_start/>Substantial heterogeneity was observed across the studies. <sentence_start/>PCR-based methods yielded higher detection rates than culture, though the magnitude of the difference varied between pathogens. <sentence_start/>Pathogen occurrence was generally higher in meat from suids, except for STEC, which was more prevalent in the game meat of ruminants. <sentence_start/>Although many strains appeared to have lower pathogenic potential compared with those typically implicated in human disease, the presence of specific virulence-associated genes, serogroups, and sequence types linked to human infections indicates that game meat may act as a potential source of infection. <sentence_start/>AMR was reported in a limited number of studies. <sentence_start/>Overall, this review highlights substantial methodological variability and important data gaps, particularly regarding virulence-associated genes, genomic characterization, and AMR. <sentence_start/>More comprehensive studies spanning a broader range of ecological and production contexts are needed to strengthen the evidence base for the microbiological safety of game meat.
Introduction

Game meat consumption continues to rise worldwide (Hedman et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0047" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/vetsci7040188" pmcid="PMC7712377" pmid="33255599" count="1">2020</citation>; Mukanganwa, Sukmawati, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0076" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2025</citation>; Ayaz et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0008" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1541-4337.70420" pmcid="PMC12949643" pmid="41762644" count="1">2026</citation>). <sentence_start/>Among the hunted ungulate species, commonly hunted deer include the white-tailed deer (<italic>Odocoileus virginianus</italic>) in North America (Goguen and Riley <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0045" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2020</citation>; Hedman et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0047" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/vetsci7040188" pmcid="PMC7712377" pmid="33255599" count="1">2020</citation>), fallow <italic>(Dama dama</italic>) and red deer (<italic>Cervus elaphus</italic>) in Australia and New Zealand (Forsyth et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0038" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2023</citation>), sika deer (<italic>C. nippon</italic>) in Japan (Okuda et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0083" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2022</citation>), and roe (<italic>Capreolus capreolus</italic>) and red deer in Europe (ENETWILD-consortium et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0050" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2021</citation>; FACE <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0034" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Other hunted ungulates include the moose (<italic>Alces alces</italic>) and chamois (<italic>Rupicara rupicara/R. pyrenaica</italic>) in Europe, along with African antelopes such as the impala (<italic>Aepyceros melampus</italic>), springbok (<italic>Antidorcas marsupialis</italic>), and greater kudu (<italic>Tragelaphus strepsiceros</italic>) (Ndlovu et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0078" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Wild boars (<italic>Sus scrofa</italic>) are especially notable for their near-global distribution across Europe, Asia, and the Americas (Markov et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0069" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2022</citation>; Kartika et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0056" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2025</citation>).

Since ancient times, hunting has been an important activity for obtaining food. <sentence_start/>Today, hunting remains a significant source of food in many rural and traditional communities (HLPE <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0049" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2017</citation>), but it is also a popular leisure activity globally (Hedman et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0047" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/vetsci7040188" pmcid="PMC7712377" pmid="33255599" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>In recent decades, hunted wild game meat has gained interest due to its culinary value, high nutritional quality, and sustainability (Costa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0023" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2016</citation>; Corradini et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0022" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.meatsci.2022.108955" pmid="36088748" count="1">2022</citation>; Ndlovu and Lebopa <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0079" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2026</citation>). <sentence_start/>It is characterized by high-quality proteins, low fat content, and a favorable fatty acid profile compared with conventional livestock meat (Bureš et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0015" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jsfa.6950" pmid="25298298" count="1">2015</citation>; Viganò et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0114" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4081/ijfs.2019.7724" pmcid="PMC6452084" pmid="31008084" count="1">2019</citation>), while also generating lower greenhouse gas emissions than beef production (Fiala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0035" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>It is often perceived as more ethical and healthier due to the natural living conditions and absence of veterinary drug use (Costa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0023" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2016</citation>; Marescotti et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0067" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, concerns remain regarding animal welfare (Dickson et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0027" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2009</citation>) and, most importantly, food safety (Marescotti et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0068" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods10010174" pmcid="PMC7830238" pmid="33467073" count="1">2021</citation>; Ranucci et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0097" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods10071548" pmcid="PMC8306536" pmid="34359418" count="1">2021</citation>; Mukanganwa, Mukuma, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0075" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Game meat production differs substantially from conventional systems, with several factors affecting microbiological safety. <sentence_start/>Warm and rainy weather, heavier animals, and delayed evisceration are associated with increased bacterial contamination of carcasses (Hedman et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0047" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/vetsci7040188" pmcid="PMC7712377" pmid="33255599" count="1">2020</citation>; Ranucci et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0097" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods10071548" pmcid="PMC8306536" pmid="34359418" count="1">2021</citation>). <sentence_start/>Indeed, field evisceration and suboptimal transport and storage conditions may increase bacterial contamination (Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2018.09.011" pmid="30497611" count="1">2019</citation>; Ayaz et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0008" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1541-4337.70420" pmcid="PMC12949643" pmid="41762644" count="1">2026</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition, the involvement of untrained hunters and the frequent absence of official inspection, particularly in informal markets (Hedman et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0047" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/vetsci7040188" pmcid="PMC7712377" pmid="33255599" count="1">2020</citation>; Ranucci et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0097" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods10071548" pmcid="PMC8306536" pmid="34359418" count="1">2021</citation>; Mukanganwa, Mukuma, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0075" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2025</citation>) or meat intended for personal consumption (Hedman et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0047" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/vetsci7040188" pmcid="PMC7712377" pmid="33255599" count="1">2020</citation>), further complicate the implementation of adequate hygiene standards. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, proper hygiene is essential because wild animals can host foodborne zoonotic pathogens such as <italic>Salmonella</italic> spp., Shiga toxin-producing <italic>Escherichia coli</italic> (STEC), <italic>Listeria</italic> spp., enteropathogenic <italic>Yersinia</italic> spp., and <italic>Campylobacter</italic> spp. <sentence_start/>(Hedman et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0047" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/vetsci7040188" pmcid="PMC7712377" pmid="33255599" count="1">2020</citation>; Altissimi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0003" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods12081689" pmcid="PMC10137515" pmid="37107481" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Campylobacteriosis and salmonellosis are among the most reported zoonoses causing gastroenteritis worldwide (EFSA and ECDC <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0030" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2903/j.efsa.2025.9759" pmcid="PMC12686834" pmid="41377167" count="1">2025</citation>; Walter et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0115" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3201/eid3104.240913" pmcid="PMC11950263" pmid="40133035" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic>L. monocytogenes</italic> may cause septicemia and death in immunocompromised individuals (Quereda et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0096" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/21505594.2021.1975526" pmcid="PMC8496543" pmid="34612177" count="1">2021</citation>), is widespread in the environment, including soil and water, and can persist in food processing environments (Tuytschaever et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0112" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1541-4337.13219" pmid="37548605" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Among <italic>Yersinia</italic> spp., only <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> and <italic>Y. pseudotuberculosis</italic> are regarded as human enteropathogenic species (Fredriksson-Ahomaa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0040" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, most <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> strains isolated from food belong to biotype 1A, which typically carry the <italic>yst</italic>B gene but lack virulence-associated genes such as the <italic>ail</italic> and <italic>yst</italic>A genes. <sentence_start/>These strains are therefore regarded as non or very low pathogenic (Terentjeva et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0109" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens11010037" pmcid="PMC8778217" pmid="35055985" count="1">2022</citation>), although some biotype 1A strains have been associated with human disease. <sentence_start/>STEC can cause hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), with disease severity largely depending on the virulence profile of the strain, particularly <italic>stx</italic> gene variants and the presence of the <italic>eae</italic> gene (Karmali et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0055" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.vetmic.2009.04.011" pmid="19410388" count="1">2010</citation>).

In addition to pathogen occurrence and characterization, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as an important One Health concern. <sentence_start/>Although wildlife is generally not exposed to antimicrobial treatments to the same extent as food-producing animals, wild animals can acquire resistant bacteria through environmental exposure (Pătrînjan et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0088" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/antibiotics15050475" pmcid="PMC13203504" pmid="42192697" count="1">2026</citation>). <sentence_start/>Consequently, the occurrence of antimicrobial-resistant foodborne pathogens in game meat remains relevant from food safety and public health perspectives.

Despite their importance, existing data on these pathogens in the game meat of hunted ungulates are highly fragmented and highly heterogeneous in study design and methodology, limiting comparability. <sentence_start/>This systematic review therefore aims to synthesize the available global evidence on the occurrence of <italic>Salmonella</italic>, <italic>Listeria</italic>, STEC, <italic>Yersinia</italic>, and <italic>Campylobacter</italic> in the game meat of hunted ungulates, along with estimating prevalence and identifying gaps in current evidence and assessing the pathogenic potential of reported isolates. <sentence_start/>By integrating worldwide data, this review provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge and highlights priorities for future research.
Methods
Search Strategy and Selection Criteria

On January 28, 2025, a literature search was conducted using Google Scholar, PubMed, and Scopus. <sentence_start/>The search was limited to articles published from 2004 onwards, corresponding to approximately the most recent 20-year period. <sentence_start/>This restriction was applied to focus on evidence generated under contemporary hunting practices, meat handling procedures, and pathogen detection methodologies that are most relevant for current food safety assessments. <sentence_start/>The search string combined target host species, matrix, and pathogen keywords as follows: [deer OR chamois OR moose OR elk OR (wild AND boar) OR (hunted AND ungulate)] AND [meat OR carcass OR carcase OR organ OR offal OR liver] AND [<italic>Salmonella</italic> OR <italic>Campylobacter</italic> OR <italic>Yersinia</italic> OR stec OR <italic>Listeria</italic>] (Appendix Table S1). <sentence_start/>The search results were exported to Rayyan software (Ouzzani et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0085" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13643-016-0384-4" pmcid="PMC5139140" pmid="27919275" count="1">2016</citation>) for screening and duplicate removal using the built-in deduplication tool. <sentence_start/>Titles and abstracts were independently screened by two reviewers (MFA and SB), and discrepancies were discussed until consensus was obtained with a third reviewer (IVD). <sentence_start/>If the abstract lacked sufficient detail to assess eligibility, the record was retained for full-text screening. <sentence_start/>Next, six reviewers (MFA, IVD, BFK, IS, JP, MC) screened the full-text articles for eligibility. <sentence_start/>The following inclusion criteria were used: (i) studies conducted after 2004, (ii) target pathogens, that is, <italic>Salmonella</italic> spp., <italic>Campylobacter</italic> spp., <italic>Yersinia</italic> spp., STEC, or <italic>Listeria</italic> spp., (iii) samples from carcasses, cut meat and meat products, or edible offal, and (iv) hunted wild animals belonging to the suids or ruminants. <sentence_start/>The exclusion criteria were: (i) studies on non-target pathogens, (ii) samples from blood, tonsils, or feces, (iii) review papers; (iv) studies involving farmed or captive animals; and (v) duplicate records.

Following the initial screening and characterization of eligible studies, we observed that most included publications originated from Europe and predominantly involved species commonly hunted in European settings. <sentence_start/>To assess whether relevant studies from other geographical regions may have been missed because of species-specific terminology, a supplementary search was performed using additional host-species terms representing hunted ungulates and game meat sources commonly reported outside Europe. <sentence_start/>The review question, databases, pathogen terms, matrix terms, screening procedures, and eligibility criteria remained unchanged. <sentence_start/>The supplementary search used the following terms for host species: (antelope OR muntjac OR impala OR springbok OR wildebeest OR duiker OR reindeer OR buffalo OR bison OR ibex OR caribou OR (feral AND (hog OR pig)) OR bushmeat). <sentence_start/>This supplementary search was performed using the same approach as the initial search. <sentence_start/>All records retrieved through the additional search were screened and assessed using the same predefined eligibility criteria as applied in the primary search to ensure methodological consistency.

The study selection process for both the initial and additional searches, including the number of records identified, screened, excluded (with reasons), and included in the final synthesis, followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines (Page et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0086" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.n71" pmcid="PMC8005924" pmid="33782057" count="1">2021</citation>) and is summarized in the PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1).
FIGURE 1

PRISMA flow diagram for study selection. <sentence_start/>An additional search was carried out, using different host species. <sentence_start/>Records that were included/excluded during the additional search are indicated with asterisk (*).
Data Extraction and Analysis

The initial data extraction was performed by five reviewers (BFK, IS, JP, MC, MFA). <sentence_start/>Each publication was assigned to one reviewer. <sentence_start/>A data extraction form was developed in Excel to capture information from the articles that met the inclusion criteria after full-text screening. <sentence_start/>The following data were extracted: bibliographic details (first author; year of publication), study context (country where the study was conducted), population characteristics (animal species), sample information (matrix, i.e., carcass, raw meat, processed meat, edible offal, or other; sample type, i.e., destructive or swab), pathogen data (genus, species, serotype, virulence genes, sequence types, AMR), detection method (culture or/and molecular), outcomes (number of samples tested, number of positive samples, prevalence estimates). <sentence_start/>As individual publications could report data for multiple pathogens, animal species, matrices, or detection methods, each unique combination was recorded as a separate observation in the database. <sentence_start/>These observations are hereafter referred to as “studies” throughout this manuscript. <sentence_start/>For the analysis, animal species were grouped into two taxonomic categories: suids and ruminant species.

To reduce errors in data collection, the final data extraction of the main outcome variables was performed independently by two reviewers per publication using a standardized extraction form. <sentence_start/>Pre-filled contextual variables from the initial database were provided for each study to support the process. <sentence_start/>For each study, the following variables were extracted: number of tested samples, number of positive samples using molecular methods, and number of positive samples using culture methods. <sentence_start/>Four reviewers (MFA, BFK, JP, IS) were randomly assigned to the publications using a block design, and each paper was reviewed by two independent reviewers, blinded to each other's results. <sentence_start/>Discrepancies between data were adjudicated by a third reviewer (IVD).

Bias risk was assessed by one reviewer (JP) using the Joanna Biggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist for Prevalence Studies (Munn et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0077" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/XEB.0000000000000054" pmid="26317388" count="1">2015</citation>) using eight questions, covering sampling frame, sampling method, sample size adequacy, description of study subjects and setting, coverage of the identified sample, validity of pathogen identification methods, consistency of measurement, and appropriateness of statistical analysis. <sentence_start/>The results for each appraisal domain are provided in Appendix Table S2. <sentence_start/>Each study was scored, and those with a score lower than four were re-evaluated by the review team. <sentence_start/>Inclusion of these studies was decided collectively on a case-by-case basis, considering the methodological limitations and their potential impact on the review.
Statistical Analysis

All analyses and visualizations were performed using R version 4.4.2. <sentence_start/>For each pathogen, prevalence data were modeled separately using a generalized linear mixed-effects model (GLMM) with a binomial distribution and logit link. <sentence_start/>The outcome variable was the number of positive samples out of the total tested. <sentence_start/>Studies reporting zero positive samples were retained in all analyses. <sentence_start/>The detection method (culture vs. PCR), animal group (ruminants vs. suids), and their interactions were included as fixed effects. <sentence_start/>Considerable heterogeneity was evident across studies, reflected by the wide variation in prevalence estimates, differences in study populations, sampling matrices, geographical regions, and diagnostic methodologies. <sentence_start/>To account for part of this heterogeneity, publication-level random effects were included in the models. <sentence_start/>To account for non-independence among observations originating from the same publication, publication was included as a random intercept. <sentence_start/>Alternative random-effects structures were explored during model development, including nested study-level effects and publication-level random slopes; however, these more complex models frequently resulted in singular fits and did not improve model fit. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the more parsimonious model was retained. <sentence_start/>Model diagnostics were evaluated using simulation-based residual analyses implemented in the DHARMa package, and no evidence of substantial overdispersion was detected. <sentence_start/>All models were fitted using maximum likelihood with Laplace approximation, as implemented in the glmer function from the lme4 package (Bates et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0011" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>For each fitted model, estimated marginal means were obtained using the emmeans package (Lenth <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0061" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Estimated marginal means were calculated on the response (probability) scale and reported by detection method (culture and PCR) within each animal group (suids and ruminants) to derive the pooled prevalence with corresponding 95% confidence intervals. <sentence_start/>Contrasts for each fixed effect (detection method and animal group) were calculated marginalized over the levels of the other effect. <sentence_start/>In addition, all pairwise comparisons across combinations of method and animal groups were performed using the default Tukey adjustment for multiple testing.
Results
Search and Selection Process

Our initial literature search retrieved 764 articles from three databases (Figure 1). <sentence_start/>After removal of 210 duplicates, the titles and abstracts of 554 articles were screened for eligibility by two independent reviewers. <sentence_start/>After consensus discussion with a third reviewer regarding 35 conflicts, a total of 357 records that did not meet the inclusion criteria were excluded. <sentence_start/>The remaining 197 records underwent full-text review, of which 154 were excluded, mostly because of the wrong sample type (<italic>n</italic> = 65), not reporting a prevalence outcome (<italic>n</italic> = 28), or because they were review papers (<italic>n</italic> = 24) (Figure 1).

The second search, using additional host species, retrieved 330 records, 32 of which were assessed for eligibility (Figure 1). <sentence_start/>Most publications were excluded because the animals were not wild and/or hunted (<italic>n</italic> = 23). <sentence_start/>Three publications from the additional search were included in the review (Bachand et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0009" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7589/0090-3558-48.3.785" pmid="22740547" count="1">2012</citation>; Haindongo et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0046" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.12834/VetIt.1228.6844.3" pmid="30574994" count="1">2018</citation>; Nkosi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0081" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2022</citation>), and nine individual studies were extracted from these three publications.
Study Characteristics

In total, 46 publications met the inclusion criteria (Appendix Table S3). <sentence_start/>They were carried out in 23 countries, mostly in Europe (<italic>n</italic> = 37), of which the vast majority were performed in Italy (<italic>n</italic> = 21). <sentence_start/><italic>Salmonella</italic> was the most frequently studied pathogen (<italic>n</italic> = 34 publications), followed by <italic>Listeria</italic> (<italic>n</italic> = 15), STEC (n = 15), <italic>Yersinia</italic> (<italic>n</italic> = 14), and <italic>Campylobacter</italic> (<italic>n</italic> = 11). <sentence_start/>Several publications reported results for more than one pathogen (<italic>n</italic> = 23). <sentence_start/>Animal species were classified as suids or ruminants, resulting in 23 publications on suids, eight on ruminants, and 15 publications including both groups. <sentence_start/>Out of the 38 publications reporting data on meat from wild suids, most studied meat from wild boars (<italic>n</italic> = 36), and only one each from warthogs (<italic>Phacochoerus aethiopicus</italic>) (Kabwang a Mpalang et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0053" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2013</citation>) and red river hogs (<italic>Potamochoerus porcus</italic>) (Bachand et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0009" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7589/0090-3558-48.3.785" pmid="22740547" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>For ruminants, the most frequently studied meat was from red deer (<italic>n</italic> = 11), followed by roe deer (<italic>n</italic> = 9), chamois (<italic>n</italic> = 6), and white-tailed deer (<italic>n</italic> = 3). <sentence_start/><italic>Salmonella</italic>, <italic>Yersinia</italic>, and <italic>Campylobacter</italic> were more frequently studied from the meat of hunted suids than from ruminants, whereas STEC and <italic>Listeria</italic> were reported in the meat of hunted ruminants and suids at similar frequencies (Appendix Table S4).

Carcasses were the most studied game meat matrix (<italic>n</italic> = 22 publications), followed by cut meat and meat products (<italic>n</italic> = 15 publications) and edible offal (<italic>n</italic> = 12 publications) (Appendix Table S5). <sentence_start/>Cut meat and meat products included raw meat cuts, ground/minced meat, and dried and smoked meat products. <sentence_start/><italic>Campylobacter</italic>, <italic>Salmonella</italic>, <italic>Yersinia</italic>, and <italic>Listeria</italic> were studied most often from carcass meat samples. <sentence_start/>STEC was most frequently studied from cut meat and meat products. <sentence_start/>Liver was by far the most frequently studied edible offal, being included in 11 out of 12 publications reporting offal samples. <sentence_start/>In three publications, multiple offal types were examined, namely liver and spleen (Cilia et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0018" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10020093" pmcid="PMC7909251" pmid="33498307" count="1">2021</citation>), liver, lungs and spleen (Conedera et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0021" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2014</citation>), and spleen and kidneys (Fredriksson-Ahomaa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0042" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10393-020-01509-5" pmcid="PMC8192372" pmid="33326058" count="1">2020</citation>).

The prevalence of foodborne bacteria in game meat had been studied using culture-based detection methods involving enrichment and selective isolation procedures (<italic>n</italic> = 30 publications), PCR detection combined with isolation (<italic>n</italic> = 13), PCR detection only (<italic>n</italic> = 7), or enzyme-linked fluorescent immunoassay (ELFA) screening followed by isolation (<italic>n</italic> = 2). <sentence_start/>For <italic>Salmonella</italic>, <italic>Listeria</italic>, and <italic>Yersinia</italic>, culturing with isolation was the most frequently used method (Appendix Table S6). <sentence_start/>For STEC detection, PCR screening followed by isolation was mostly used. <sentence_start/>For <italic>Campylobacter</italic>, both culturing and PCR-based methods were used with similar frequency.

To evaluate the bias risk, each publication was scored across eight domains. <sentence_start/>Of the 46 included publications, the majority had a score of 8 (<italic>n</italic> = 20) or 7 (<italic>n</italic> = 11), while 7, 5, 2, and 1 publications had a lower score of 6, 5, 4, and 3, respectively.
Pathogen Prevalence in Hunted Game Meat

<italic>Salmonella</italic> spp

A total of 82 <italic>Salmonella</italic> prevalence estimates were included in the quantitative analysis, corresponding to 64 unique studies originating from 34 publications (Figure 3). <sentence_start/>Most publications only used culture methods to detect <italic>Salmonella</italic> (<italic>n</italic> = 23). <sentence_start/>Six publications used PCR screening followed by culture (Peruzy et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0092" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2019.05.005" pmid="31100642" count="1">2019</citation>; Fredriksson-Ahomaa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0042" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10393-020-01509-5" pmcid="PMC8192372" pmid="33326058" count="1">2020</citation>; Razzuoli et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0098" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10050568" pmcid="PMC8151295" pmid="34067207" count="1">2021</citation>; Peruzy, Cristiano, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0090" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4081/ijfs.2022.9967" pmcid="PMC8883827" pmid="35284341" count="1">2022</citation>; Peruzy, Murru, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0091" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.foodcont.2021.108782" count="1">2022</citation>; Floris et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani14040562" pmcid="PMC10886018" pmid="38396530" count="1">2024</citation>), and two publications used VIDAS immunoassay screening (Hingston et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0048" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4315/JFP-19-492" pmid="32032422" count="1">2020</citation>; Altissimi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0004" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods13081156" pmcid="PMC11049437" pmid="38672829" count="1">2024</citation>) after which culturing was performed on screening-positive samples. <sentence_start/>PCR detection and culturing were used in parallel in two publications (Kabwang a Mpalang et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0053" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2013</citation>; Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2018.09.011" pmid="30497611" count="1">2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>One publication used PCR detection only without culture (Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2023.110110" pmid="36796163" count="1">2023</citation>).

In the game meat of suids, 13 out of 31 culture-based studies reported no <italic>Salmonella</italic> positive samples, whereas prevalence among positive studies ranged from 1 to 36%. <sentence_start/>For PCR-based studies (<italic>n</italic> = 8), two studies reported no positive samples, and prevalence among positive studies ranged from 3% to 36%. <sentence_start/>Among the game meat of ruminants, 27 out of 32 culture-based studies and 8 out of 11 PCR-based studies reported no positive samples, with prevalence estimates among positive studies ranging from 0.3% to 15% and from 3% to 5%, respectively. <sentence_start/>In suid game meat, the pooled prevalence estimates were 1.7% (95% CI 0.8%-3.6%) based on culture methods and 3.7% (1.7%-7.6%) based on PCR results. <sentence_start/>The pooled prevalence in ruminant game meat was 0.5% (0.2%-1.3%) using culture methods and 1.3% (0.4%-3.7%) using PCR-based results. <sentence_start/>The odds of having a positive result were significantly higher using PCR than using culture methods (OR = 2.4, <italic>p</italic> = 0.001) and in suid meat than in ruminant meat (OR = 3.3, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001).

The highest <italic>Salmonella</italic> prevalence rates (32% and 36%) were obtained in wild boar meat from southern Italy by PCR (Peruzy et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0092" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2019.05.005" pmid="31100642" count="1">2019</citation>; Peruzy, Cristiano, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0090" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4081/ijfs.2022.9967" pmcid="PMC8883827" pmid="35284341" count="1">2022</citation>). <sentence_start/>Culture confirmation of PCR-positive samples was high, resulting in similarly elevated prevalence estimates using culture methods (27% and 36%, respectively). <sentence_start/>A high prevalence (25%) by culturing was also reported in wild boar meat from Albania (Elezi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0033" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic>Salmonella</italic> prevalence estimates in the meat of wild ruminants were generally low (0%-5%) with both PCR and culturing, except for Nkosi et al. (<citation rid="crf370657-bib-0081" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2022</citation>), who reported a culture-based prevalence of 15% in impala meat around shot wounds in South Africa.

<italic>S. enterica</italic> subspecies and serotypes were reported in 14 publications. <sentence_start/>However, characterization of isolates from ruminant game meat was limited because <italic>Salmonella</italic> was only rarely isolated from these samples. <sentence_start/>Consequently, only two publications reported characterized isolates from ruminant meat: <italic>S. enterica</italic> subspecies <italic>houtenae</italic> was isolated from a chamois liver in Italy (Giorda et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0044" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2014</citation>) and <italic>S. enterica</italic> subspecies <italic>enterica</italic> serotype Corvalis from a deer carcass in Spain (Díaz-Sánchez et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0025" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.vetmic.2012.12.026" pmid="23384892" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>In contrast, more extensive characterization results were available for isolates from suid game meat. <sentence_start/>Razzuoli et al. (<citation rid="crf370657-bib-0098" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10050568" pmcid="PMC8151295" pmid="34067207" count="1">2021</citation>) identified all six subspecies (<italic>arizonae, diarizonae, enterica, houtenae, indica</italic>, and <italic>salamae</italic>) in suid livers, of which subspecies <italic>enterica</italic> was the most common, followed by <italic>salamae</italic> and <italic>diarizonae</italic>. <sentence_start/>In total, 30 serotypes of the subspecies <italic>enterica</italic> were identified in suid meat, as reported in 13 publications (Table 1). <sentence_start/>The most common serotypes were Typhimurium, Stanleyville, and Enteritidis, which were reported by ten, four, and three publications, respectively.
STEC

The reported STEC prevalence estimates ranged from 0% to 100% across 50 extracted prevalence estimates corresponding to 34 unique studies, extracted from 15 publications (Figure 4). <sentence_start/>The STEC prevalence estimates of one publication were excluded because sample screening was based on the VIDAS immunoassay targeting only serotype O157:H7 without screening the <italic>stx</italic> genes (Hingston et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0048" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4315/JFP-19-492" pmid="32032422" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>In ruminant game meat, 5 out of 13 culture-based studies and 4 out of 20 PCR-based studies reported no STEC-positive samples. <sentence_start/>Among studies reporting positive samples, prevalence ranged from 0.8% to 50% and 0.8% to 100%. <sentence_start/>In suid game meat, 3 of 8 culture-based studies and 3 of 9 PCR-based studies reported no positives, whereas prevalence estimates among positive studies ranged from 4% to 14% and 16% to 64%, respectively. <sentence_start/>Model-based pooled estimates indicated a higher prevalence in ruminant meat (culture 5.6% [2.3%-13.4%]; PCR 18.3% [8.1%-36.2%]) than in suid meat (culture 2.4% [0.9%-6.2%]; PCR 11.6% [4.9%-25.4%]). <sentence_start/>The odds of finding a positive sample were significantly higher when using PCR than culture (OR = 4.5; <italic>p</italic> < 0.001) and lower in the meat of suids than that of ruminants (OR = 0.5; <italic>p</italic> < 0.001).

Concerning STEC detection, the methods applied varied greatly among the studies, which likely contributed to the large variations in the outcomes. <sentence_start/>Most publications (9 out of 15) used PCR screening followed by culture, five used PCR detection without culture, and one only used culture methods (Figure 4).

Nine studies combined a PCR screening step followed by the culturing of presumptive-positive samples targeting <italic>stx1</italic>/<italic>stx2</italic> (Díaz-Sánchez et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0026" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2012.09.016" pmid="23177058" count="1">2012</citation>, Díaz-Sánchez et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0025" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.vetmic.2012.12.026" pmid="23384892" count="1">2013</citation>; Peruzy, Cristiano, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0090" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4081/ijfs.2022.9967" pmcid="PMC8883827" pmid="35284341" count="1">2022</citation>; Peruzy, Murru, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0091" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.foodcont.2021.108782" count="1">2022</citation>; (<citation rid="crf370657-bib-0082" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-30333-4" pmcid="PMC9957979" pmid="36828872" count="1">2023</citation>) in game meat from roe deer (39%), red deer (15%), and wild boar (12%) originating from multiple European countries.

Five publications relied solely on the PCR detection of enriched samples. <sentence_start/>These publications targeted either <italic>stx1</italic>/<italic>stx2</italic> (Fredriksson-Ahomaa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0042" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10393-020-01509-5" pmcid="PMC8192372" pmid="33326058" count="1">2020</citation>; Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2018.09.011" pmid="30497611" count="1">2019</citation>, <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2023.110110" pmid="36796163" count="1">2023</citation>) or <italic>stx1</italic>/<italic>stx2</italic> in combination with <italic>eae</italic> (Magwedere et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0066" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/1040638713477407" pmid="23512921" count="1">2013</citation>; Haindongo et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0046" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.12834/VetIt.1228.6844.3" pmid="30574994" count="1">2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>Within these publications, presumptive STEC prevalence estimates ranged from 0% in the meat of American bison (<italic>Bison bison</italic>), red deer, and reindeer in the United States, to 100% in the carcasses of wildebeest (<italic>Chonnocaetes taurinus</italic>) and greater kudu in Namibia (Magwedere et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0066" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/1040638713477407" pmid="23512921" count="1">2013</citation>; Haindongo et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0046" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.12834/VetIt.1228.6844.3" pmid="30574994" count="1">2018</citation>), though the latter results should be interpreted with caution due to the limited sample size (<italic>n</italic> = 5 each). <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, the same authors also found high prevalence estimates from the carcasses of springbok (78%, <italic>n</italic> = 41) and gemsbok (<italic>Oryx gazella</italic>) (69%, <italic>n</italic> = 75).

Thierry et al. (<citation rid="crf370657-bib-0110" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2020.108589" pmid="32442794" count="1">2020</citation>) used a culture method without prior PCR screening to isolate STEC from rusa deer (<italic>C. timorensis</italic>) meat samples from Mauritius, using a chromogenic STEC agar (CHROMagar STEC) after non-selective enrichment, followed by PCR confirmation of colonies targeting <italic>stx1</italic>, <italic>stx2</italic>, and <italic>eae</italic>. <sentence_start/>STEC carrying <italic>stx</italic>2 was isolated from 5 out of 61 (8%) rusa deer meat samples.

12%) (Díaz-Sánchez et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0026" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2012.09.016" pmid="23177058" count="1">2012</citation>, <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0025" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.vetmic.2012.12.026" pmid="23384892" count="1">2013</citation>; Nüesch-Inderbinen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0082" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-30333-4" pmcid="PMC9957979" pmid="36828872" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Both <italic>stx</italic>1 and <italic>stx</italic>2 were found, but <italic>stx</italic>2 was predominant (82/102; 80%), occurring alone (71/102; 70%) or in combination with <italic>stx</italic>1 (14/102; 14%). <sentence_start/>In four publications, s<italic>tx</italic> gene subtyping was performed on 84 isolates. <sentence_start/>The most common subtype was <italic>stx</italic>2b (46/84; 55%), mainly alone (38/46; 83%) or combined with <italic>stx</italic>1c (5/46; 11%) or <italic>stx</italic>1d (3/46; 6.5%). <sentence_start/>Other subtypes (s<italic>tx</italic>1c, <italic>stx</italic>1d, <italic>stx</italic>2a, <italic>stx</italic>2e, and <italic>stx</italic>2g) were less frequent (1%-15%; Table 2). <sentence_start/>The <italic>eae</italic> gene was detected in 12% (12/102) of STEC isolates, exclusively found in the livers of chamois (3 isolates carrying <italic>stx</italic>2b) and roe deer (9 isolates carrying <italic>stx</italic>1a, <italic>stx</italic>1d, <italic>stx</italic>2b, and/or <italic>stx</italic>2) in Italy (Listorti et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0063" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens13070576" pmcid="PMC11279605" pmid="39057803" count="1">2024</citation>).

Nüesch-Inderbinen et al. (<citation rid="crf370657-bib-0082" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-30333-4" pmcid="PMC9957979" pmid="36828872" count="1">2023</citation>) applied serotyping, virulotyping, and MLST on 27 STEC isolates from 23 game meat samples in Central Europe and revealed that ST738, ST812, and ST753 were the most prevalent (Table 2), identifying ST738 and ST812 in roe deer meat from Germany, Poland, and Switzerland and ST753 in red deer meat from Slovenia and Switzerland. <sentence_start/>ST738 was also identified in wild boar meat from Switzerland. <sentence_start/>In particular, STEC O146:H28 ST738 (<italic>n</italic> = 10) harboring <italic>stx</italic>2b were detected in both roe deer and wild boar meat, STEC O110:H31 ST812 (<italic>n</italic> = 5) harboring <italic>st</italic>1c + <italic>stx</italic>1c or <italic>stx</italic>2b were found in roe deer meat and STEC O27:H30 ST 753 (<italic>n</italic> = 3) harboring <italic>stx</italic>2b were isolated from red deer meat in Slovenia and Switzerland. <sentence_start/>Thierry et al. (<citation rid="crf370657-bib-0110" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2020.108589" pmid="32442794" count="1">2020</citation>) sequenced one isolate from rusa meat in Mauritius, which was identified as O146, ST738.
