Sannö et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0102" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani13193055" pmcid="PMC10571951" pmid="37835661" count="1">2023</citation>; Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2023.110110" pmid="36796163" count="1">2023</citation>, Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2018.09.011" pmid="30497611" count="1">2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>A high prevalence (31%) of <italic>ail</italic>-positive <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> was reported in minced wild boar meat in Sweden (Sannö et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0102" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani13193055" pmcid="PMC10571951" pmid="37835661" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>A clearly lower prevalence of <italic>ail</italic>-positive <italic>Yersinia</italic> (including both <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> and <italic>Y. pseudotuberculosis</italic>) were reported in the meat of white-tailed deer (9%) and moose (6%) in Finland (Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2018.09.011" pmid="30497611" count="1">2019</citation>, <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2023.110110" pmid="36796163" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Three publications used the <italic>yst</italic>B and <italic>yst</italic>A genes to detect non- or low-pathogenic (biotype 1A) and pathogenic (biotypes 1B, 2-5) <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic>, respectively (Peruzy et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0092" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2019.05.005" pmid="31100642" count="1">2019</citation>; Peruzy, Cristiano, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0090" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4081/ijfs.2022.9967" pmcid="PMC8883827" pmid="35284341" count="1">2022</citation>; Peruzy, Murru, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0091" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.foodcont.2021.108782" count="1">2022</citation>). <sentence_start/>The prevalence was lower in studies using <italic>yst</italic>A compared with <italic>yst</italic>B. <sentence_start/>The detection rates using <italic>yst</italic>A varied between 0% and 21%, whereas the detection rates using <italic>yst</italic>B varied between 14% and 75%.

<italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> was isolated in 16 studies, extracted from nine publications (Table 3). <sentence_start/>Most of the isolates belonged to biotype 1A and carried the <italic>yst</italic>B gene. <sentence_start/>In some studies, biotypes 1B and 2 were identified (Mignone et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0071" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2015</citation>; Bancerz-Kisiel et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0010" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tvjl.2015.08.010" pmid="26626093" count="1">2016</citation>; Modesto et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0073" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10040398" pmcid="PMC8065425" pmid="33801613" count="1">2021</citation>). <sentence_start/>The <italic>ail</italic> and <italic>yst</italic>A virulence genes were reported in some <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> studies (Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2018.09.011" pmid="30497611" count="1">2019</citation>; Modesto et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0073" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10040398" pmcid="PMC8065425" pmid="33801613" count="1">2021</citation>; Floris et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani14040562" pmcid="PMC10886018" pmid="38396530" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>Biotype 1A isolates found in wild boar livers from Italy were frequently <italic>ail-</italic> (44%) or <italic>yst</italic>A- (20%) positive (Modesto et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0073" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10040398" pmcid="PMC8065425" pmid="33801613" count="1">2021</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic>Y. pseudotuberculosis</italic> serotype O1, carrying the <italic>virF</italic> gene on the virulence plasmid, was isolated in one study, from wild boar kidney/spleen samples (Fredriksson-Ahomaa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0042" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10393-020-01509-5" pmcid="PMC8192372" pmid="33326058" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>All isolates carried both chromosomal and plasmid-borne virulence genes. <sentence_start/>In some studies, <italic>Yersinia</italic> isolates were sequenced (Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2018.09.011" pmid="30497611" count="1">2019</citation>; Floris et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani14040562" pmcid="PMC10886018" pmid="38396530" count="1">2024</citation>; Siddi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods13010065" pmcid="PMC10778173" pmid="38201093" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>Several sequence types were identified among <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> isolates. <sentence_start/>All sequence types were unknown types or types not associated with human infections. <sentence_start/><italic>Y. pseudotuberculosis</italic> isolates belonged to sequence type ST42.
<italic>Campylobacter</italic> spp

A total of 24 <italic>Campylobacter</italic> prevalence estimates were included in the quantitative analysis, corresponding to 18 unique studies originating from 11 publications (Figure 7). <sentence_start/>Five publications used a combination of PCR and culture methods, five used culture methods only, and one used PCR detection only. <sentence_start/>For suid game meat, 3 of 10 culture-based studies and 1 of 4 PCR-based studies reported no <italic>Campylobacter</italic> detection. <sentence_start/>Among studies reporting at least one positive sample, prevalence estimates ranged between 1% and 27%, and 5% to 27%, respectively. <sentence_start/>For ruminants, 3 of 5 culture-based studies and none of five PCR-based studies reported no positives, with prevalence estimates among positive studies ranging from 9% to 19%, and 2% to 22%, respectively. <sentence_start/>The pooled prevalence estimates were consistently higher in the meat of hunted suids, that is, 3.9% (95% CI: 1.8%-8.5%) using culture and 5.1% (2.1%-11.7%) using PCR, than in ruminant meat, which reached 1.8% (0.1%-4.5%) using culture and 2.5% (1.0%-6.0%) using PCR. <sentence_start/>Although PCR-based methods yielded numerically higher prevalence estimates than culture-based methods, the difference was not statistically significant (OR = 1.3, <italic>p</italic> = 0.21). <sentence_start/>Meat from wild suids was associated with higher odds of positive <italic>Campylobacter</italic> findings (OR = 2.1, <italic>p</italic> = 0.002) than meat from ruminants. <sentence_start/>High <italic>Campylobacter</italic> prevalence estimates were reported in game meat from Central Africa (DRC) (Kabwang a Mpalang et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0053" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>The highest prevalence was found in smoked meat from warthog (26%) with both PCR and culture methods.

In two publications, <italic>Campylobacter</italic> was identified only at the genus level (Mignone et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0071" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2015</citation>; Stella et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0107" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4315/0362-028X.JFP-18-077" pmid="30118347" count="1">2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>In four other publications, the species of <italic>Campylobacter</italic> were determined (Table 4). <sentence_start/><italic>C. coli</italic> was detected in all studies and was reported as the predominant species in smoked game meat from ruminants and suids in DRC (Kabwang a Mpalang et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0053" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic>C. jejuni</italic> was identified in four publications, while <italic>C. lanienae</italic> was found in wild boar liver and carcass samples in one publication (Ziomek et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0120" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods12040778" pmcid="PMC9956588" pmid="36832850" count="1">2023</citation>).
Antimicrobial Resistance

AMR in foodborne bacteria isolated from game meat was reported in nine publications, which were all performed in Europe. <sentence_start/>AMR was assessed in isolates of <italic>Salmonella</italic>, STEC, <italic>Listeria</italic>, and <italic>Yersinia</italic> (Table 5). <sentence_start/>The presence of resistance genes was reported in three publications (Nüesch-Inderbinen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0082" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-30333-4" pmcid="PMC9957979" pmid="36828872" count="1">2023</citation>; Floris et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani14040562" pmcid="PMC10886018" pmid="38396530" count="1">2024</citation>; Siddi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods13010065" pmcid="PMC10778173" pmid="38201093" count="1">2024</citation>).

<italic>Salmonella</italic> isolates from wild boar meat exhibited highly variable AMR profiles, ranging from fully susceptible to highly resistant (Bonardi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0013" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10344-021-01531-0" pmcid="PMC8475815" pmid="34602932" count="1">2021</citation>; Cilia et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0018" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10020093" pmcid="PMC7909251" pmid="33498307" count="1">2021</citation>; Razzuoli et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0098" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10050568" pmcid="PMC8151295" pmid="34067207" count="1">2021</citation>; Siddi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods13010065" pmcid="PMC10778173" pmid="38201093" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>Resistance to streptomycin, sulfonamides, and tetracycline was frequently observed. <sentence_start/>One isolate (<italic>S</italic>. Infantis) was multi-drug resistant (MDR) (Cilia et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0018" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10020093" pmcid="PMC7909251" pmid="33498307" count="1">2021</citation>).

AMR in STEC from game meat was investigated in three publications (Díaz-Sánchez et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0026" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2012.09.016" pmid="23177058" count="1">2012</citation>; Nüesch-Inderbinen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0082" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-30333-4" pmcid="PMC9957979" pmid="36828872" count="1">2023</citation>; Listorti et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0063" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens13070576" pmcid="PMC11279605" pmid="39057803" count="1">2024</citation>), one of which employed whole-genome sequencing to detect AMR genes (Nüesch-Inderbinen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0082" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-30333-4" pmcid="PMC9957979" pmid="36828872" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Based on phenotypic analyses, STEC isolates were generally susceptible to all tested antimicrobials (Table 5), except for one MDR isolate reported by Listorti et al. (<citation rid="crf370657-bib-0063" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens13070576" pmcid="PMC11279605" pmid="39057803" count="1">2024</citation>) showing resistance to cefotaxime, ceftazidime, ciprofloxacin, colistin, gentamicin, meropenem, nalidixic acid, and sulfamethoxazole. <sentence_start/>Molecular analyses revealed the presence of the cephalosporinase-encoding gene <italic>bla</italic> <sub>EC</sub> in STEC isolates from Austria, Hungary, Poland, Slovenia, and Switzerland (Nüesch-Inderbinen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0082" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-30333-4" pmcid="PMC9957979" pmid="36828872" count="1">2023</citation>).

AMR was reported in two <italic>L. monocytogenes</italic> isolates, both of which were positive for genes coding for fosfomycin resistance (Floris et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani14040562" pmcid="PMC10886018" pmid="38396530" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>AMR in <italic>Yersinia</italic> isolates was studied in three publications (Modesto et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0073" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10040398" pmcid="PMC8065425" pmid="33801613" count="1">2021</citation>; Floris et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani14040562" pmcid="PMC10886018" pmid="38396530" count="1">2024</citation>; Siddi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods13010065" pmcid="PMC10778173" pmid="38201093" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>Most of the isolates were resistant to β-lactams, including penicillins (ampicillin and amoxicillin) and first-generation cephalosporins (Table 5). <sentence_start/>Frequent resistance to sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim was also reported (Modesto et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0073" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10040398" pmcid="PMC8065425" pmid="33801613" count="1">2021</citation>).
Discussion
Study Limitations and Identification of Data Gaps

This systematic review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the available evidence on the prevalence and virulence-associated genes of bacterial zoonotic pathogens in hunted game meat while also identifying key data gaps in the current evidence base. <sentence_start/>Although the dataset was sufficiently large to support meaningful comparisons, notable gaps were identified for certain pathogens, particularly <italic>Campylobacter</italic>, for which relatively few studies were available.

The geographical distribution of available studies was highly uneven, with most publications originating from Europe and particularly Italy. <sentence_start/>An additional search including host species relevant to non-European hunting systems identified only three additional eligible publications. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the limited geographical representation appears to reflect a genuine evidence gap rather than a major limitation of the search strategy. <sentence_start/>This finding itself is important, as it highlights the lack of information from large parts of Africa, Asia, the Americas, and Oceania.

Statistical modeling was constrained by the limited number of publications available for several pathogens and by the uneven distribution of studies across geographical regions, matrices, and sampling stages. <sentence_start/>Consequently, the analyses focused on the predefined factors of primary interest, namely detection method and animal group, while avoiding more highly parameterized models that could lead to unstable estimates.

Our search was restricted to studies published from 2004 onwards. <sentence_start/>Although this allowed the review to focus on evidence generated during the most recent two decades, relevant historical studies may have been excluded. <sentence_start/>Consequently, data extending beyond this period could not be evaluated.

Finally, detailed characterization of isolates, including WGS, virulence-associated genes, serotyping, and AMR profiling was available for only a minority of studies. <sentence_start/>This limits the extent to which pathogen occurrence can be linked to public-health relevance.
Methodological Considerations and Diagnostic Limitations

A key finding of this review is that methodological choices significantly influenced reported prevalence estimates. <sentence_start/>Molecular and culture-based methods each have distinct advantages and limitations. <sentence_start/>In several publications, PCR was used as an initial screening tool due to its rapidity, cost-effectiveness, and high analytical sensitivity, enabling the detection of bacterial DNA even in injured or viable non-culturable cells. <sentence_start/>However, PCR-based approaches may underestimate prevalence when inhibitors (e.g., hemoglobin and myoglobin, lipids, proteins) are present in complex matrices, such as meat, leading to false-negative results (Fredriksson-Ahomaa and Korkeala <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0041" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/CMR.16.2.220-229.2003" pmcid="PMC153140" pmid="12692095" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>Conversely, reliance solely on culture-based methods may also underestimate the true occurrence of pathogens, since stressed bacteria due to chilling, drying, or processing or viable but non-culturable cells may escape detection (Kabwang a Mpalang et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0053" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2013</citation>; Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2018.09.011" pmid="30497611" count="1">2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>Importantly, PCR does not provide information on bacterial viability, and PCR-positive findings should therefore not automatically be interpreted as evidence of viable pathogenic organisms. <sentence_start/>Studies that do not include culture confirmation may therefore overestimate the occurrence of pathogens. <sentence_start/>This limitation is particularly relevant when broad genetic markers are targeted, as these may also detect nonpathogenic strains. <sentence_start/>Consequently, methodological choices, including the selection of target genes and the use of confirmatory culture, strongly influence reported prevalence estimates and their interpretation in a public health context.

Across the studies, PCR-based methods generally yielded higher detection rates than culture-based methods. <sentence_start/>However, the magnitude and statistical significance of this difference varied among pathogens, which provides insight into pathogen-specific diagnostic challenges. <sentence_start/>The larger discrepancies observed for STEC and <italic>Yersinia</italic> suggest that analytical choices, including molecular target selection and limitations of available isolation methods, may strongly influence the resulting prevalence estimates. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the smaller differences observed for <italic>Listeria</italic> indicate greater agreement between molecular and culture-based approaches. <sentence_start/>While the sole use of culture-based methods was most frequent for <italic>Salmonella</italic>, <italic>Listeria</italic>, and <italic>Yersinia</italic>, a combination of PCR and culture was more common for STEC and <italic>Campylobacter</italic>.

For <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic>, the choice of the PCR target gene had a pronounced effect on the reported prevalence. <sentence_start/>As such, the highest <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> prevalence (75%) was observed using a PCR assay targeting the <italic>yst</italic>B gene (Peruzy, Cristiano, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0090" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4081/ijfs.2022.9967" pmcid="PMC8883827" pmid="35284341" count="1">2022</citation>), which has been shown to be carried by nonpathogenic <italic>Yersinia</italic> spp. and non- or low-pathogenic <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> 1A (Imori et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0051" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.micpath.2017.01.008" pmid="28062290" count="1">2017</citation>; Joutsen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0052" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.vetmic.2020.108798" pmid="32768239" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>By contrast, a substantially lower prevalence estimate (21%) was obtained when targeting <italic>yst</italic>A, which is associated with pathogenic <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic>. <sentence_start/>These findings underscore the importance of selecting virulence-associated markers, such as the <italic>ail</italic> and <italic>ystA</italic> genes, to ensure that PCR-based detection reflects the presence of pathogenic <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic>. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, the high PCR-based prevalence estimates reported using pathogenic markers should be interpreted as evidence of widespread detection of virulence-associated genetic markers rather than direct evidence of viable pathogenic <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic>. <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, PCR-positive results for <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> were infrequently confirmed by culture (Fredriksson-Ahomaa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0042" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10393-020-01509-5" pmcid="PMC8192372" pmid="33326058" count="1">2020</citation>; Peruzy, Cristiano, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0090" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4081/ijfs.2022.9967" pmcid="PMC8883827" pmid="35284341" count="1">2022</citation>; Peruzy, Murru, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0091" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.foodcont.2021.108782" count="1">2022</citation>), which is partially attributable to the limited sensitivity of available culture methods for enteropathogenic <italic>Yersinia</italic>, which complicates the isolation and identification of pathogenic strains (Van Damme et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0113" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2013.05.007" pmid="24010595" count="1">2013</citation>; Fredriksson-Ahomaa <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0039" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/978-3-031-27164-9_8" count="1">2023</citation>).

Particularly for STEC, the odds of detecting a positive sample were significantly higher with PCR than using culture. <sentence_start/>PCR screening of enrichment broths targeting the <italic>stx</italic> and <italic>eae</italic> genes often identified a substantial proportion of positive samples, though subsequent isolation rates were low (Nüesch-Inderbinen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0082" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-30333-4" pmcid="PMC9957979" pmid="36828872" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Consequently, PCR-based detection primarily reflects the presence of STEC-associated genetic markers, whereas public-health assessment requires isolation of viable strains. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, the isolation of STEC remains essential, as it enables detailed characterization of strains and assessment of their public health relevance. <sentence_start/>Although PCR methods may overestimate prevalence, the detection of STEC isolates is well known to be very difficult due to their similar morphology to (abundant) apathogenic <italic>E. coli</italic> on common media for <italic>Enterobacteriaceae</italic> (such as MacConkey agar and TBX agar) and even on chromogenic selective media (such as CHROMagar STEC).

For <italic>L. monocytogenes</italic>, detection predominantly relied on culture-based methods, either alone or in combination with PCR. <sentence_start/>Although PCR-based methods in the current study showed significantly higher odds of detecting <italic>Listeria</italic> than culture-based methods, the effect size was modest and smaller than observed for <italic>Salmonella</italic>, STEC, or <italic>Yersinia</italic>. <sentence_start/>In studies employing both approaches, a high proportion of PCR-positive samples were confirmed by culture, suggesting that culture methods for <italic>L. monocytogenes</italic> are comparatively sensitive (Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2018.09.011" pmid="30497611" count="1">2019</citation>; Fredriksson-Ahomaa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0042" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10393-020-01509-5" pmcid="PMC8192372" pmid="33326058" count="1">2020</citation>; Floris et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani14040562" pmcid="PMC10886018" pmid="38396530" count="1">2024</citation>).

For <italic>Salmonella</italic>, PCR-based methods also yielded higher detection estimates, although the effect was smaller than observed for STEC and <italic>Yersinia</italic>. <sentence_start/>This may indicate that conventional culture protocols, despite their widespread use, may underestimate <italic>Salmonella</italic> occurrence in complex matrices such as game meat, as high levels of background bacteria could hinder the enrichment and detection of <italic>Salmonella</italic> (Neyaz et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0080" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2024</citation>).

For <italic>Campylobacter</italic>, PCR and culture were used at similar frequencies. <sentence_start/>Although PCR-based detection generally yielded higher prevalence estimates than culture-based approaches, the difference was not statistically significant in the final models. <sentence_start/>This discrepancy between PCR and culture is consistent with the pathogen's known fastidious growth requirements (Park <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0087" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0168-1605(01)00678-x" pmid="11981968" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, background flora has also been shown to grow on classical <italic>Campylobacter-</italic>selective media (Yoo et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0119" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2014.07.032" pmid="25126968" count="1">2014</citation>) and can reduce the sensitivity of culture-based methods (Abulreesh et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0001" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.watres.2005.05.004" pmid="15979120" count="1">2005</citation>; Neyaz et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0080" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>High prevalence estimates in warthog and duiker meat based on combined PCR and culture methods indicate a substantial presence of viable <italic>Campylobacter</italic>, suggesting a genuinely elevated risk of human exposure rather than methodological overestimation within the specific studies and conditions analyzed.

To conclude, PCR offers a rapid and sensitive screening tool but may lead to overestimation or misinterpretation of public health risk if not carefully designed and interpreted, particularly when non-virulence-associated targets are used. <sentence_start/>Culture methods, while essential for confirming viability and enabling characterization, may underestimate prevalence due to methodological limitations. <sentence_start/>Therefore, an integrated approach combining PCR with targeted, virulence-associated markers and subsequent culture confirmation is critical for generating accurate and meaningful prevalence data for properly assessing the associated public health risks. <sentence_start/>Moreover, beyond the distinction between PCR-based and culture-based methods, substantial heterogeneity existed in the analytical protocols themselves. <sentence_start/>Studies differed in enrichment procedures, selective media, PCR formats, primer and probe sets, and the extent of isolate characterization. <sentence_start/>Such methodological differences likely contributed to variability in prevalence estimates and complicate direct comparison between studies.
Pathogenic Potential and Characterization of Detected Isolates

A major limitation across the included studies is the insufficient characterization of isolates, which constrains the assessment of their public health relevance. <sentence_start/>In many cases, pathogen identification was not complemented by detailed analyses, such as virulence gene profiling, serotyping, or genomic characterization, limiting insights into their pathogenic potential and their relatedness to strains causing human disease. <sentence_start/>In addition, available data were confined to a small number of countries that performed such characterization.

Particularly for <italic>Yersinia</italic> spp., pathogenicity using chromosomal or plasmid-associated virulence genes was not always assessed. <sentence_start/>Quite high isolation rates (12%-19%) of <italic>Yersinia</italic> spp. <sentence_start/>were found in the game meat of suids and ruminants, though most isolates had no or limited pathogenic potential based on the available virulence-associated markers. <sentence_start/>The isolates predominantly belonged to <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> biotype 1A carrying the <italic>yst</italic>B gene, which is typically associated with nonpathogenic strains. <sentence_start/>By contrast, virulence determinants, such as <italic>ail</italic> and <italic>yst</italic>A, which are associated with pathogenic strains of <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic>, were only sporadically detected in isolates from wild boar offal, moose and deer carcasses, and deer livers. <sentence_start/>Moreover, these <italic>ail</italic>-positive isolates could not clearly be classified into any pathogenic biotype, and the presence of virulence plasmid-encoded genes, such as <italic>virF</italic> and <italic>yadA</italic>, which is essential for full pathogenicity, were not reported. <sentence_start/>Nonpathogenic <italic>ail</italic>-positive <italic>Yersinia</italic> isolates, including <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> and <italic>Y. kristensenii</italic>, have been found in wild animals (Joutsen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0052" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.vetmic.2020.108798" pmid="32768239" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>Genotypic analyses indicated that sequence types of <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> biotype 1A isolates from game meat differed from the types typically associated with human infections (Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2018.09.011" pmid="30497611" count="1">2019</citation>; Floris et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani14040562" pmcid="PMC10886018" pmid="38396530" count="1">2024</citation>; Siddi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods13010065" pmcid="PMC10778173" pmid="38201093" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>Isolates reported as biotype 1B were sporadically described in wild boar carcasses and livers from Poland and Italy. <sentence_start/>These isolates primarily carried <italic>ystB</italic> and lacked several virulence determinants. <sentence_start/>Because reliable distinction between biotypes 1A and 1B is challenging using phenotypic tests, and biotype determination was not supported by genomic characterization, the available data do not allow confirmation that classical highly pathogenic biotype 1B strains were present. <sentence_start/>Consequently, the pathogenic significance of these isolates should be interpreted with caution. <sentence_start/>Notably, <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic> bioserotype 4/O3, which predominates domestic pigs, pork, and human yersiniosis cases, was not identified in any of the publications. <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that game meat is unlikely to represent a major source of pathogenic <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic>. <sentence_start/>However, the detection of <italic>Y. pseudotuberculosis</italic> serotype O1 carrying the virulence plasmid-associated <italic>vir</italic>F genes was found in wild boar offal (Fredriksson-Ahomaa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0042" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10393-020-01509-5" pmcid="PMC8192372" pmid="33326058" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>These strains belonged to sequence type ST42, which has been associated with human infections in Europe.

For STEC, the pathogenic potential can be assessed through the identification of virulence-associated genes, including <italic>stx</italic> and <italic>eae</italic> (World Health Organization <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0118" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2019</citation>; EFSA Biohaz Panel et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0058" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2020</citation>; Lindqvist et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0062" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2023</citation>) as well as through genomic characterization (Blankenship et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0012" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/microorganisms11051298" pmcid="PMC10224053" pmid="37317272" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Particularly <italic>stx</italic>2a and <italic>stx</italic>2d are strongly associated with severe human disease, including HUS (Lindqvist et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0062" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2023</citation>; EFSA and ECDC <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0030" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2903/j.efsa.2025.9759" pmcid="PMC12686834" pmid="41377167" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Only two isolates detected in game meat from red deer in Spain (Díaz-Sánchez et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0026" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2012.09.016" pmid="23177058" count="1">2012</citation>) and wild boar in Switzerland (Nüesch-Inderbinen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0082" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-30333-4" pmcid="PMC9957979" pmid="36828872" count="1">2023</citation>) harbored high-risk genomic profiles (i.e., <italic>eae</italic>-/<italic>stx</italic>2a+). <sentence_start/>STEC isolates from game meat in the current study were generally characterized by virulence profiles that are less frequently associated with severe human disease. <sentence_start/>Most isolates harbored <italic>stx2</italic> with a clear predominance of the <italic>stx</italic>2<italic>b</italic> subtype, while <italic>eae</italic> was only rarely detected. <sentence_start/>The absence of <italic>eae</italic> suggests that these strains may rely on alternative adhesion factors for intestinal colonization, such as <italic>lpfA</italic> (long polar fimbriae A) (Torres et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0111" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/JCM.00566-09" pmcid="PMC2725649" pmid="19494071" count="1">2009</citation>) and <italic>iha</italic> (IrgA homologue adhesin) (Colello et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0020" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.heliyon.2019.e03015" pmcid="PMC6920203" pmid="31879713" count="1">2019</citation>), which were carried by 70% and 78% of the STEC sequenced by Nüesch-Inderbinen et al. (<citation rid="crf370657-bib-0082" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-30333-4" pmcid="PMC9957979" pmid="36828872" count="1">2023</citation>), respectively. <sentence_start/>The most common virulence gene profile observed in isolates from wild ungulate meat was <italic>eae</italic>-/<italic>stx</italic>2b+, which is generally considered to have a lower virulence compared with profiles typically associated with severe human disease. <sentence_start/>This is further supported by serotyping. <sentence_start/>The major STEC serogroups most frequently implicated in human infections, commonly referred to as the “Top 7” (O26, O45, O103, O111, O121, O145, and O157) (EFSA and ECDC <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0030" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2903/j.efsa.2025.9759" pmcid="PMC12686834" pmid="41377167" count="1">2025</citation>), were rarely detected in game meat

Most STEC isolates from game meat harbored virulence gene profiles that are less frequently associated with severe human disease. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, the presence of specific serogroups, sequence types, and virulence determinants reported among human clinical isolates were identified, demonstrating that game meat can contain strains with recognized pathogenic potential.

The isolation rate of <italic>Listeria</italic> spp. was high in wild boar carcasses in one study (Stella et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0107" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4315/0362-028X.JFP-18-077" pmid="30118347" count="1">2018</citation>); however, no <italic>L. monocytogenes</italic> was identified, highlighting the importance of species-level identification for assessing the public health risk. <sentence_start/>For <italic>L. monocytogenes</italic>, serogroup IIa was the most frequently identified serogroup in this review. <sentence_start/>Serogroup IIa is a frequent type among both human and food isolates, but the proportion is significantly higher among food isolates (Suominen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0108" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/S0950268823001073" pmcid="PMC10468812" pmid="37424309" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>By contrast, serogroup IVb, which is more often associated with severe human listeriosis and outbreaks, was only rarely detected in game meat. <sentence_start/>Game meat has been implicated in <italic>L. monocytogenes</italic> outbreaks using MLST (Filipello et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0036" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2020.103433" pmid="32138991" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>Available data on sequence types were very limited in this review, but several game meat sequence types have been associated with human listeriosis (Fredriksson-Ahomaa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0043" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods11223679" pmcid="PMC9689155" pmid="36429271" count="1">2022</citation>), indicating that isolates from game meat may pose a public health risk. <sentence_start/>However, the limited availability of whole genome sequence (WGS) data constrains comprehensive conclusions.

<italic>S. enterica</italic> subspecies <italic>enterica</italic> was the most frequently identified subspecies in wild boar meat, though the other five subspecies were also reported. <sentence_start/>A wide variety of <italic>Salmonella</italic> serotypes were reported, with <italic>S</italic>. Typhimurium, <italic>S</italic>. Enteritidis, <italic>S</italic>. Coeln, <italic>S</italic>. Thompson and <italic>S</italic>. Newport being among the most frequent. <sentence_start/>Importantly, several of these serotype are also among the leading causes of human salmonellosis (EFSA and ECDC <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0029" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2903/j.efsa.2024.9106" pmcid="PMC11629028" pmid="39659847" count="1">2024</citation>), indicating that game meat may harbor strains with established relevance for human disease. <sentence_start/>However, data on isolate characterization in the current study was limited. <sentence_start/>Similarly, several outbreaks that have been associated with game meat lacked molecular confirmation connecting human and game meat derived isolates (Kuhn et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0060" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21596006" count="1">2011</citation>; Madar et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0065" ref-type="bibr" pmcid="PMC3313773" pmid="22454811" count="1">2012</citation>; Draper et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0028" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.33321/cdi.2025.49.010" pmid="39965608" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Overall, the available characterization data indicate that game meat may harbor pathogens with demonstrated public health relevance, but the lack of comprehensive genomic characterization and source attribution studies limits definitive conclusions regarding transmission to humans.

Species-level identification of <italic>Campylobacter</italic> isolates indicates that <italic>C. coli</italic> was the dominant species in game meat, including smoked products, across both suids and ruminants. <sentence_start/>However, <italic>C. jejuni</italic>, a major human pathogen, was also consistently detected, albeit less frequently, highlighting its relevance for food safety (Kabwang a Mpalang et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0053" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Its occurrence, particularly in insufficiently heat-treated products, such as smoked meat, underscores a potential risk to consumers (Kabwang a Mpalang et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0053" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition, the detection of <italic>C. lanienae</italic> points to the broader diversity of <italic>Campylobacter</italic> species in game meat. <sentence_start/>Although its public health significance is less well understood, its presence alongside <italic>C. coli</italic> and <italic>C. jejuni</italic> in wild boar offal, including the liver, suggests that game meat may serve as a reservoir for multiple <italic>Campylobacter</italic> species.

Across all investigated pathogens, a consistent limitation is the insufficient characterization of isolates with respect to virulence determinants, serogroups, and genomic profiles. <sentence_start/>While many isolates detected in game meat appear to have a lower pathogenic potential compared with those commonly associated with human disease, the presence of specific virulence factors, serogroups, and sequence types linked to human infections indicate that game meat cannot be excluded as a potential source of transmission. <sentence_start/>Clear epidemiological links between game meat consumption and human illness are rarely established, and available genomic data remain limited. <sentence_start/>This highlights the need for more comprehensive surveillance, including WGS and virulence gene profiling.
Matrix and Sampling Stage

Comparing prevalence estimates across studies was not only constrained by analytical methods, but also by substantial heterogeneity in the sample matrices and sampling stages. <sentence_start/>The type of matrix analyzed (e.g., carcass swabs, muscle tissue, offal, or processed products) and the point of sampling along the production chain (hunting site, processing, or retail) represent different combinations of primary contamination, cross-contamination, and potential bacterial growth during storage. <sentence_start/>Consequently, the prevalence estimates reported in this review should not be interpreted as representing a single stage of the game-meat chain. <sentence_start/>Instead, they reflect occurrence in meat sampled at different points, ranging from carcasses immediately after hunting to retail products. <sentence_start/>The pooled prevalence estimates should therefore be interpreted as indicators of pathogen occurrence rather than direct measure of consumer exposure.

Several studies included in this review suggested that carcass contamination may be influenced by factors related to hunting and field dressing practices, including shooting accuracy, time to evisceration, carcass handling, and hygiene during transport and processing (Atanassova et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0006" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.meatsci.2007.07.004" pmid="22062460" count="1">2008</citation>; Avagnina et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0007" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.meatsci.2012.01.025" pmid="22386324" count="1">2012</citation>; Mirceta et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0072" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2017</citation>; Stella et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0107" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4315/0362-028X.JFP-18-077" pmid="30118347" count="1">2018</citation>; Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2018.09.011" pmid="30497611" count="1">2019</citation>; Branciari et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0014" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods9081076" pmcid="PMC7465837" pmid="32784708" count="1">2020</citation>; Cenci-Goga et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0017" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2020</citation>; Nkosi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0081" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2022</citation>; Peruzy, Murru, et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0091" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.foodcont.2021.108782" count="1">2022</citation>). <sentence_start/>Likewise, studies sampling meat at processing or retail stages reflect not only field contamination but also the effects of subsequent handling, processing, packaging, storage, and opportunities for cross-contamination (Ranucci et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0097" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods10071548" pmcid="PMC8306536" pmid="34359418" count="1">2021</citation>; Bonardi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0013" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10344-021-01531-0" pmcid="PMC8475815" pmid="34602932" count="1">2021</citation>; Sauvala et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2023.110110" pmid="36796163" count="1">2023</citation>; Kabwang a Mpalang et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0053" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2013</citation>).

The variation observed between studies is therefore likely to reflect a combination of biological differences, hunting practices, processing conditions and analytical methodology. <sentence_start/>However, because most studies investigated only a single matrix at a single stage of the production chain, the independent effects of matrix type and sampling stage could not be quantified reliably. <sentence_start/>This limitation likely contributed substantially to the heterogeneity observed across prevalence estimates. <sentence_start/>Despite these limitations, the available evidence consistently supports the importance of hygienic field dressing practices, minimization of fecal contamination during carcass handling, and adequate hygiene and temperature control during processing and storage to reduce contamination risks throughout the game-meat chain.
Influence of Animal Groups

Across pathogens, a consistent pattern emerged in which prevalence estimates were generally higher in meat from suids than from wild ruminants, with the notable exception of STEC. <sentence_start/>These differences likely reflect differences in ecology, behavior, and gastrointestinal physiology between the two host groups.

Wild boars exhibit omnivorous and opportunistic feeding behavior, including rooting and scavenging, which increases exposure to a wide range of environmental and fecal contaminants (Carlos et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0016" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.onehlt.2023.100598" pmcid="PMC10372376" pmid="37520846" count="1">2023</citation>), facilitating pathogen acquisition and transmission of enteric pathogens. <sentence_start/>In line with this, our results indicate that wild boar meat represents a more important source of <italic>Salmonella</italic> compared with ruminant game meat, for which the prevalence was consistently low. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, considerable variation exists, and low prevalence in suis has also been reported (Mirceta et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0072" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2017</citation>; Petrovic et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0093" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2024</citation>), suggesting that beyond host ecology, factors such as hunting hygiene also play an important role. <sentence_start/>The importance of suids in the epidemiology of <italic>Salmonella</italic> and <italic>Yersinia</italic> is further supported by their recognized role as reservoirs in domestic pigs.

By contrast, STEC showed a different pattern, with a higher prevalence in ruminant game meat compared with suids. <sentence_start/>This is consistent with the well-established role of domestic ruminants as major reservoirs of STEC (Mughini-Gras et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0074" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/zph.12403" pmid="28921940" count="1">2018</citation>; Pires et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0095" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/S095026881900116X" pmcid="PMC6625198" pmid="31364563" count="1">2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>Host-specific adaptations facilitating long-term intestinal colonization likely explain why STEC is more strongly associated with ruminant game than with meat from suids (Kudva and Stasko <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0059" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1746-6148-9-266" pmcid="PMC3878412" pmid="24373611" count="1">2013</citation>; Matthews et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0070" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/S0950268805004590" pmcid="PMC2870353" pmid="16409660" count="1">2006</citation>; Segura et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12866-021-02343-7" pmcid="PMC8524897" pmid="34663220" count="1">2021</citation>).

In this systematic review, <italic>L. monocytogenes</italic> was reported in the game meat of both suids and ruminants, showing that game meat can be a source of <italic>L. monocytogenes</italic>. <sentence_start/>While most studies reported relatively low prevalence estimates (< 8%), occasional high prevalence rates were reported in both ruminant and suid game meat. <sentence_start/><italic>L. monocytogenes</italic> is ubiquitous in soil, which may reflect the higher prevalence in suids. <sentence_start/>However, given the importance of post-harvest contamination and bacterial growth for this pathogen, differences between host species should be interpreted with caution. <sentence_start/>Regarding <italic>Yersinia</italic>, the prevalence was significantly higher in suid meat compared with ruminants. <sentence_start/>Wild suids commonly eat rodents and birds, which frequently carry and transmit <italic>Yersinia</italic> in their intestinal tract. <sentence_start/>In African settings, the predominance of <italic>C. coli</italic> may be linked to its association with suids and wildlife, combined with informal meat production practices, such as bushmeat processing, limited hygiene, and insufficient heat treatment, which facilitate contamination and bacterial survival. <sentence_start/>This is further supported by clinical data from Ghana (Karikari et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0054" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2017</citation>), where <italic>C. coli</italic> accounted for 37% of all isolates and was the predominant species in patients with gastroenteritis (46%), highlighting its significant role in human infections in the region.
Antimicrobial Resistance

Although AMR was not the primary focus of this review and available data were limited, the detection of antimicrobial-resistant foodborne pathogens in game meat remains relevant because these bacteria may be transmitted to consumers or food handlers. <sentence_start/>AMR data were reported in a limited number of studies, so interpretation of these findings requires caution. <sentence_start/>Bacteria isolated from game meat may reflect contamination originating from the animal itself, environmental sources, or processing-related cross-contamination. <sentence_start/>Consequently, the available data in this review do not allow robust conclusions regarding the role of wildlife as reservoirs of AMR.

For <italic>Salmonella</italic>, reported resistance profiles in wild boar meat ranged from fully susceptible to resistant isolates, with variability likely reflecting both regional differences and limited sample sizes. <sentence_start/>In general, AMR in <italic>Salmonella</italic> is known to depend on geographical location, source, and serotype (Wang et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0116" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-59758-3" pmcid="PMC12085583" pmid="40382325" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Resistance to older antimicrobials, such as streptomycin, sulfonamides, and tetracycline, was relatively common, whereas resistance to critically important antimicrobials for human medicine, including fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins, remained rare (Cilia et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0018" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10020093" pmcid="PMC7909251" pmid="33498307" count="1">2021</citation>; Razzuoli et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0098" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10050568" pmcid="PMC8151295" pmid="34067207" count="1">2021</citation>). <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, evidence from wild boar feces suggests that higher AMR levels, including resistance to critically important antimicrobials, may occur (Akwongo et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0002" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12917-024-04462-5" pmcid="PMC11724570" pmid="39799360" count="1">2025</citation>), highlighting the potential for carcass contamination under inadequate hygiene conditions.

For STEC, AMR data were particularly scarce and indicated a predominantly susceptible phenotype. <sentence_start/>Only a single MDR isolate was reported (Listorti et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0063" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens13070576" pmcid="PMC11279605" pmid="39057803" count="1">2024</citation>), while other isolates were fully susceptible. <sentence_start/>The detection of chromosomal <italic>bla</italic> <sub>EC</sub> genes in STEC from game meat (Nüesch-Inderbinen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0082" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-30333-4" pmcid="PMC9957979" pmid="36828872" count="1">2023</citation>) suggests the potential for resistance to third-generation cephalosporins; however, their phenotypic expression was not assessed. <sentence_start/>Overall, these findings contrast with higher resistance levels reported in STEC and commensal <italic>E. coli</italic> from conventional meat sources (Rega et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0099" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/microorganisms9020214" pmcid="PMC7912124" pmid="33494307" count="1">2021</citation>; EFSA and ECDC <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0031" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2903/j.efsa.2026.p240203" pmcid="PMC12914650" pmid="41717217" count="1">2026</citation>), indicating that game meat may currently represent a less important reservoir of AMR in this pathogen.

Very limited information was available for <italic>L. monocytogenes</italic>, with AMR assessed in only two isolates (Floris et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani14040562" pmcid="PMC10886018" pmid="38396530" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>Genes coding for fosfomycin resistance were detected in both isolates. <sentence_start/>Fosfomycin resistance is considered intrinsic to the species and is therefore of limited clinical relevance (Fredriksson-Ahomaa et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0043" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods11223679" pmcid="PMC9689155" pmid="36429271" count="1">2022</citation>; Díaz-Martínez et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0024" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/1040841X.2024.2412007" pmid="39404832" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>One isolate showed resistance to cefotaxime and nalidixic acid, two clinically critical antimicrobials. <sentence_start/>Similarly, for <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic>, much of the observed resistance, particularly to β-lactams, can be attributed to intrinsic mechanisms, including chromosomal <italic>bla</italic> genes (Koskinen et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0057" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fmicb.2022.841841" pmcid="PMC8967395" pmid="35369517" count="1">2022</citation>; Siddi et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/foods13010065" pmcid="PMC10778173" pmid="38201093" count="1">2024</citation>) and the chromosomal <italic>vat</italic>F gene for streptogramin resistance (Floris et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ani14040562" pmcid="PMC10886018" pmid="38396530" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>When intrinsic resistance was excluded, acquired resistance and MDR appeared to be uncommon, although sporadic MDR isolates have been reported (Modesto et al. <citation rid="crf370657-bib-0073" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/pathogens10040398" pmcid="PMC8065425" pmid="33801613" count="1">2021</citation>).
Public Health Relevance

The occurrence of foodborne pathogens in game meat should not be interpreted directly as consumer risk. <sentence_start/>Public health risk depends not only on pathogen prevalence, but also on bacterial viability, concentration in food, pathogenic characteristics of the strains present, preparation practices, consumption patterns, and the susceptibility of the exposed population. <sentence_start/>Consequently, the prevalence estimates reported in this review should be regarded as indicators of potential exposure rather than direct measures of public health risk.

The public health relevance differed between pathogens. <sentence_start/>For <italic>Salmonella</italic>, several serotypes identified in game meat overlapped with those frequently associated with human salmonellosis, suggesting that game meat may act as a vehicle for strains relevant to human health. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the available evidence for <italic>Yersinia</italic> indicated that most isolates belonged to biotype 1A or lacked key virulence-associated markers, whereas the biotypes most commonly associated with human yersiniosis were rarely or never detected. <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that game meat is unlikely to represent a major source of classical pathogenic <italic>Y. enterocolitica</italic>, although sporadic detection of pathogenic <italic>Yersinia</italic> species demonstrates that transmission remains possible.

For STEC, most characterized isolates harbored virulence profiles that are less frequently associated with severe human disease than those commonly reported from cattle. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, isolates carrying virulence-associated genes, serogroups, and sequence types linked to human disease were identified, indicating that game meat cannot be excluded as a potential source of clinically relevant STEC. <sentence_start/>Likewise, <italic>L. monocytogenes</italic> isolates primarily belonged to serogroups commonly found in food, while highly pathogenic outbreak-associated serogroups were reported only sporadically. <sentence_start/>However, given the ability of <italic>L. monocytogenes</italic> to survive and grow during refrigerated storage, even relatively low contamination levels may be relevant under unfavorable storage conditions.

The public health significance of <italic>Campylobacter</italic> remains difficult to assess because only a limited number of studies were available. <sentence_start/>The detection of both <italic>C. jejuni</italic> and <italic>C. coli</italic> demonstrates that recognized human pathogens can occur in game meat, but insufficient data currently exist to demonstrate the relative importance of game meat as a transmission route.

AMR was only sporadically reported and multidrug-resistant isolates were uncommon. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, the detection of multidrug-resistant <italic>Salmonella</italic>, STEC, and <italic>Yersinia</italic> isolates demonstrates that game meat may contribute to environmental pathways for the dissemination of AMR and highlights the value of continued surveillance.
Conclusions

This systematic review demonstrates that hunted game meat can be contaminated with zoonotic bacterial pathogens capable of causing disease in consumers. <sentence_start/>However, the magnitude of this contribution of game meat is difficult to assess due to the limited number of available studies, particularly for <italic>Campylobacter</italic>. <sentence_start/>The substantial heterogeneity among included studies investigating <italic>Salmonella</italic>, STEC, <italic>L. monocytogenes, Yersinia</italic>, and <italic>Campylobacter</italic>, especially regarding the analytical methodologies, animal species, and sample matrices tested, the limited information on pathogenicity and characterization of most pathogens, and the various geographical areas, highlights the need for more harmonized data to enable more robust and accurate risk assessments. <sentence_start/>We therefore recommend increasing the number of studies on hunted game meat and placing greater emphasis on the characterization of isolates, particularly with respect to pathogenic potential and AMR, to better evaluate the public health significance of pathogens detected in game meat. <sentence_start/>Moreover, additional research is needed in countries and regions where game meat is commonly consumed to achieve a more comprehensive and globally representative understanding of the microbiological safety of wild game meat.
